text.en: The day of the school food festival has come, and the stalls are full of fresh fruits, sprouts, dhokla, dosa, vada, ragi laddu and many other dishes. The children taste, guess ingredients and ask why one dish tastes sweet, salty and bitter all at once. As they visit each stall they learn about the six tastes, millets, the three groups of food, junk food, water and cooking. Let us taste, think and plan a healthy plate.

At a stall called Mystery Masala the children tasted a food that was a little sweet, a little salty and a little bitter, and they wondered why it tasted different to each of them. It was Ugadi Pachadi, a traditional food of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Telangana, made with six taste elements. The six tastes are sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent. Examples are jaggery for sweet, tamarind for sour, salt for salty, green chilli for pungent, neem for bitter and raw mango for astringent. In Ayurveda the six tastes are called shad rasa, and eating balanced food with all six tastes is good for health.
Surbhi visited a stall of millet foods and remembered that her grandmother ate jowar and bajra roti in winter and jau roti in summer. Millets are rich sources of nutrients. The children enjoyed jowar upma and other millet-based foods, and ragi laddu was on the festival menu too. You can find out a millet food that is cooked in your own home.
A banner at the festival said Colours on Plate, Wellness in Life, which reminds us to eat a variety of foods. Our body needs variety to stay healthy, energetic and strong, and no single food has all the nutrients we need. Energy foods give energy, and they include rice, wheat, potato, maize, banana, honey and millets, and butter, ghee and oil. Body-building foods help us grow and make our muscles strong, and they include pulses, soybeans, chickpeas, milk, cheese, eggs, fish, meat, nuts and tofu. Protective foods protect us from diseases, and they include fruits and vegetables like carrot, orange, lemon, papaya, spinach, cabbage, guava, amla and tomato. If we ate foods from only one group every day, our body would miss the other things it needs.
A balanced plate has food from all three groups in the right amounts, with protective foods the most, then body-building foods, and some energy foods. This helps us stay healthy, active and happy, and every region of India has a thali that mixes foods with different tastes and benefits. Junk food is food that is not healthy if eaten regularly or in large amounts, because it has a lot of oil, salt and sugar. Examples are soft drinks, chips, burgers, pizza and over-processed packaged food, and fresh home-cooked food is better. A food diary for a week helps you see what you eat and which food groups you are missing.
Water is an important part of our diet. Water helps in digesting food and keeps our skin and body healthy. It also helps to remove waste from the body through urine, sweat and faeces. Water-rich fruits like watermelon and cucumber also help the body keep water, and drinking enough water should be a healthy habit.
The children wondered how the festival dishes were made, and there are different cooking methods. Idli is steamed, rice and dal are boiled, samosa and vada are fried, papad can be roasted, and cakes and breads are baked. Some foods like fruit chaat and vegetable salads can be eaten without cooking. A chef is a professional cook, and the word chef in French means a director or head of the kitchen. A solar cooker cooks food using sunlight instead of a gas stove or electricity, and it does not produce smoke or ash, so it does not pollute the environment.
Before buying or eating packaged food, check its label. A label tells the net weight, the date it was packed and the best before or expiry date, and the main ingredients. Checking labels protects us from eating spoiled food and helps us choose healthy food. You can also make a food collage with three sections for energy, body-building and protective foods, and plan your own school food festival.
